intro:
Bakery phone orders for custom cake requests work best when the call stays short, specific, and repeatable. The goal is to get the right details the first time, then send a clear ticket to the kitchen or decorator.

For a busy bakery, that usually means a simple phone script, a written list of cake options, and a way to route special requests to the right person. sections.h2: What details should you collect on a custom cake call?
sections.body:
A custom cake order can sound simple until one detail gets missed. The safest approach is to collect the same core items every time, in the same order.

Use this checklist for every bakery phone order for a custom cake:
- Customer name
- Callback phone number
- Pickup date and time
- Cake size or serving count
- Flavor
- Filling
- Frosting
- Writing on the cake
- Color or decoration notes
- Allergy-sensitive notes

A clean phone script line helps a lot. Try: "What size cake do you need, what flavor, and what would you like written on it?"

If you take different styles, ask for those too. For example:
- Sheet cake or round cake
- Buttercream or whipped frosting
- Photo or themed decoration
- Candles, sprinkles, fruit, or simple border

If your shop has limited options, say them clearly. Example: "We can do vanilla, chocolate, or red velvet for custom orders, and pickup is available after 2 p.m. tomorrow." That saves time and avoids back-and-forth.

sections.h2: How do you keep phone orders from slowing the front counter?
sections.body:
The biggest bakery problem is not just taking the order. It is taking the order while a cashier is bagging cookies, answering walk-ins, and checking the oven.

A better system is to separate quick questions from custom work. Standard pickup orders can be handled fast. Custom cakes with special writing, photos, or allergy notes should be treated like a staff review order.

A practical workflow looks like this:
1. Answer the phone with a short greeting.
2. Identify whether it is a standard order or a custom cake request.
3. Collect the order details.
4. Confirm the pickup time.
5. Send the order to the kitchen or decorator.
6. Hand off anything unusual to staff with a note.

If you use ROAL, it can answer the phone, take pickup and delivery orders from your live menu, and send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. For custom cake requests that need a human decision, it can hand the call to staff with a summary.

A simple script helps your team stay consistent: "Thanks for calling. I can take the details now. For custom artwork or allergy-sensitive requests, I’ll pass it to the team for review."

sections.h2: What should you say when a cake request needs review?
sections.body:
Some cake calls are easy. Others need a baker or manager to approve them. That includes unusual fillings, same-day large cakes, allergy-sensitive requests, or detailed decoration work.

Have a script ready so the caller does not feel bounced around. Use lines like:
- "I can take the details and have our team review it."
- "For that decoration, I want to make sure we confirm availability first."
- "Let me collect the basics and pass this to the bakery team."

Here is a simple handoff checklist for staff:
- Cake size
- Flavor and filling
- Pickup date and time
- Special writing
- Decoration notes
- Allergy concerns
- Caller name and phone

That last step matters. If the caller asks for almond-free or gluten-sensitive handling, send the request to staff with a clear summary instead of guessing.

ROAL is set up for that kind of handoff. It can answer routine questions about hours, address, parking, and the menu, but anything it cannot answer goes to an inbox. The owner answers once, and the host learns it from then on. That keeps the phone moving without forcing the machine to improvise on tricky cake work.

sections.h2: How do you price custom cakes without guessing on the phone?
sections.body:
Pricing gets messy when customers call and say, "How much is a cake?" The answer depends on size, flavor, filling, writing, and decoration. You do not need a huge pricing system to make the call smoother. You just need a few clear anchors.

Use a simple pricing chart for the phone team. Example numbers only, so plug in your own:

| Cake type | Example price | What it covers |
|---|---:|---|
| Small round cake | $28 | Basic flavor and writing |
| Half-sheet cake | $45 | Standard frosting and message |
| Custom themed cake | $65 | Extra decoration time |
| Allergy-sensitive review | Quote later | Staff must confirm ingredients |

If a caller wants something outside your normal menu, you can say: "For that style, we need to review it and call you back with a quote." That is better than guessing and then losing money.

This also helps with custom cake orders from regular customers. They already know your shop, but they still need a clear answer. A written price range at the counter and in your menu notes can reduce the number of uncertain calls.

sections.h2: How does call forwarding work for a bakery?
sections.body:
If you want an AI phone host to answer while you stay at the counter, call forwarding is the bridge. On many landlines and some carriers, dialing *72 and then the forwarding number forwards all calls, and *73 turns it off. Some mobile carriers use **21*number# for all calls and ##21# to turn it off; **61*number# can forward unanswered calls; **67*number# can forward busy calls. Verizon Wireless commonly uses *72 / *73, and *71 for busy or no-answer forwarding.

Because codes vary by carrier and plan, always confirm with your carrier and test with a real call. If you use a business VoIP system, forwarding is usually set in the web portal.

A bakery-friendly setup is often one of these:
- Forward all calls during a holiday rush
- Forward only when busy during the lunch rush
- Forward unanswered calls after a few rings
- Turn forwarding off after closing

ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically once the owner claims the host, and the restaurant keeps its own number. You can forward your existing number to it, and turn forwarding off any time. That makes it easier to test on a slow day, then use it more heavily when cake orders and pickup calls stack up.

sections.h2: What does a good bakery phone script sound like?
sections.body:
A bakery phone script should sound warm, short, and direct. The customer should know you are helping them, not grilling them.

Here is a script a cake shop can adapt:
- "Thanks for calling. How can I help with your order today?"
- "Is this for pickup, delivery, or a custom cake request?"
- "What size cake do you need, and what should we write on it?"
- "What day and time would you like to pick it up?"
- "Let me repeat that back so we make sure it is right."

A quick repeat-back catches mistakes before the cake is made. For example:
- Caller says: chocolate half-sheet, white frosting, happy birthday Maria, pickup Friday at 4.
- You repeat: "Chocolate half-sheet, white frosting, message 'Happy Birthday Maria,' pickup Friday at 4 p.m."

That kind of script matters even more when the shop is busy. If your staff cannot get to the phone, ROAL can answer, collect the order details, speak the caller’s language, and confirm the order back. It can also take reservations or pass complaints and manager requests to staff with a summary, which is useful if the same line handles cafe seating or event questions.
